$comment: Teaching content for cl_orchestration. The workflow-versus-agent distinction is the most heavily tested idea in Section 3.

knowledgePoints.name: One question separates them
knowledgePoints.teach:
Workflow — a predefined series of Claude calls solving a known problem. You can picture the exact steps ahead of time.

Agent — Claude gets a goal and a set of tools and figures out its own path. Used when you don't know what task or parameters will come in.

Can you picture the steps in advance? Yes → workflow. No → agent.

Everything else follows from that. A workflow's steps are known, so they can be tested individually, optimised individually, and reasoned about when they fail. An agent's cannot, because they do not exist until it runs.

questions.q: What single question separates a workflow design from an agent design?
options: Does the task need more than one Claude call?
Can you picture the exact steps in advance?
Does the task require tools?
Is the output structured or free-form?
questions.explain: Knowability of the steps. Both may use several calls and both may use tools.

options: Any pipeline with more than three Claude calls
A predefined series of Claude calls solving a known problem
A loop that terminates on a fixed iteration count
A single call with process steps in the prompt
questions.explain: Predefined and known — that is what makes the steps designable ahead of time.

knowledgePoints.name: The trade, and the default
knowledgePoints.teach:
BenefitsDownsides
Workflowshigher accuracy (focus per subtask), easier to test and evaluate, more predictable, better for well-defined problemsless flexible, more constrained UX, more upfront design work
Agentsflexible UX, can combine tools in unexpected ways, handles novel situations, can ask for more inputlower success rate, harder to test and instrument, less predictable

Prefer workflows where possible. Only reach for agents when truly required.

The course's argument for the default is blunt: users want reliability, not a fancy agent. “Lower success rate” is not a footnote — it is the price of the flexibility, paid on every request including the ordinary ones.

questions.q: Which does the course recommend by default?
options: Agents, since they handle more cases
Workflows, reaching for agents only when truly required
Whichever is cheaper to run
Agents for user-facing work, workflows for batch
questions.explain: Workflows by default. Users want reliability, and agents trade success rate for flexibility.

questions.q: Which is a stated downside of workflows?
options: Lower success rate
More upfront design work and a more constrained UX
Harder to test
Cannot use tools
questions.explain: You pay in design effort and flexibility. Testability and predictability are what you get back.

reviewQuestions.q: Which is a benefit unique to agents?
options: Higher accuracy per subtask
Can combine tools in unexpected ways and handle novel situations
Easier to evaluate
More predictable behaviour
reviewQuestions.explain: Novelty handling is the thing you are buying. The other three are workflow advantages.

reviewQuestions.q: Why are agents harder to instrument than workflows?
options: They run on a different endpoint
The steps are not known ahead of time, so there is no fixed set of stages to measure
Their tool calls are executed server-side
They do not emit stop_reason
reviewQuestions.explain: You cannot put a metric on a stage that does not exist until runtime.

knowledgePoints.name: Fan out, then aggregate
knowledgePoints.teach:
Parallelization splits one complex task into multiple independent sub-tasks, runs them simultaneously, and aggregates the results into a final decision.

            ┌── credit check ────┐
loan app ───┼── fraud check ─────┼──→ aggregate ──→ decision
            └── affordability ───┘

The sub-tasks need not be identical — they are just meaningfully independent evaluations of the same thing.

Use it when a decision can be broken into independent evaluations. The aggregation step is part of the pattern, not an afterthought.

Two things it buys: latency, since the branches run at once, and accuracy, since each branch is a focused prompt rather than one prompt asked to weigh three concerns at the same time.

questions.q: A loan decision needs a credit check, a fraud check, and an affordability check. Which pattern, and what is the final step?
options: Routing; the final step is selecting a pipeline
Parallelization; the final step is aggregating the results into a decision
Chaining; the final step is a revision pass
Evaluator–optimizer; the final step is a grade
questions.explain: Independent evaluations run at once, then aggregated. Aggregation is part of the pattern.

options: Yes — the same prompt run on different inputs
No — they need only be meaningfully independent
Yes, unless they use different models
No, but they must return the same output schema
questions.explain: Independence is the requirement, not sameness.

reviewQuestions.q: Besides latency, what does parallelization buy?
options: Lower token cost
Accuracy, since each branch is a focused prompt rather than one prompt weighing everything
Guaranteed structured output
Fewer round trips to the API
reviewQuestions.explain: Focus per subtask — the same reason workflows generally beat one large prompt.

knowledgePoints.name: The long-prompt problem
knowledgePoints.teach:
Chaining breaks a large task into smaller sequential subtasks that build on each other.

It exists to solve one specific failure:

A single prompt with many constraints often gets some of them partially ignored.

Eight rules in one prompt reliably produces output obeying five. Not because any rule was unclear, but because attention is finite and they compete.

The two-step fix:

  1. Generate the content — imperfectly, that is expected.
  2. Revise in a focused pass targeting specific fixes only.

The second call is not the first call again. It carries the output and a short list of what to check, so nothing competes for attention.

questions.q: A prompt with eight rules obeys five of them. What pattern fixes it?
options: Parallelization — evaluate each rule independently
Chaining — generate first, then a focused revision pass targeting specific fixes
Routing — send each rule to its own pipeline
Evaluator–optimizer — grade until all eight pass
questions.explain: Chaining is the named fix for the long-prompt problem: generate, then revise with focus.

questions.q: What does the second call in a two-step chain do?
options: Re-runs the original prompt at a lower temperature
Takes the first output and revises it against specific targeted fixes
Grades the first output and returns a score
Splits the output into sections for parallel processing
questions.explain: A focused revision pass. Only a few concerns compete for attention, so they all get it.

reviewQuestions.q: How does chaining differ from parallelization?
options: Chaining is sequential and each step builds on the last; parallelization runs independent steps at once
Chaining uses one model, parallelization uses several
Chaining is for known steps, parallelization for unknown ones
Chaining aggregates results, parallelization does not
reviewQuestions.explain: Sequence and dependence versus simultaneity and independence.

reviewQuestions.q: Why does one prompt with many constraints drop some of them?
options: The API truncates long prompts
The constraints compete for finite attention, so some are only partially applied
Later instructions overwrite earlier ones
Constraints past a count of five are ignored
reviewQuestions.explain: Competition, not truncation — which is why splitting the work rather than rewording it is the fix.

knowledgePoints.name: Classify, then send down exactly one path
knowledgePoints.teach:
Routing categorises the input first — with a Claude call — then forwards it to one specialised pipeline built for that category.

                    ┌→ refund pipeline
inbox → classify ───┼→ bug-report pipeline
                    └→ sales pipeline

Input goes to exactly ONE pipeline. That is what lets each be deeply optimised for its own case.

Contrast with parallelization, where the input goes to all branches and the results are combined. Same fan shape on a diagram, opposite semantics.

The classification step is also where per-task model choice gets applied in practice: classify with Haiku, handle most categories with Sonnet, and let only the rare hard category reach Opus.

questions.q: One inbox receives refund requests, bug reports, and sales enquiries. Which pattern, and how many pipelines does a message reach?
options: Parallelization; all three
Routing; exactly one
Chaining; all three in sequence
Routing; one or more, depending on the classification confidence
questions.explain: Routing sends each input down a single branch, which is what allows each branch to specialise.

options: Routing is sequential, parallelization is not
Routing sends the input to one branch; parallelization sends it to all and aggregates
Routing requires structured output
Routing uses one model, parallelization uses several
questions.explain: One branch versus all branches. The diagrams look alike; the semantics are opposite.

reviewQuestions.q: What does the classification step in routing typically run on?
options: The same tier as the pipelines, for consistency
A cheap tier such as Haiku — classification is exactly its brief
Opus, since a misroute is expensive
A non-LLM classifier
reviewQuestions.explain: Classification is Haiku's named workload, and routing is where per-task model choice actually gets used.

knowledgePoints.name: The loop that grades its own homework
knowledgePoints.teach:
Evaluator–optimizer: a producer creates output, a grader evaluates it against criteria, and if it is rejected the feedback loops back to the producer for revision. Repeat until accepted.

produce ──→ grade ──→ accepted? ──yes──→ done
   ↑                    │
   └────── feedback ────no

The course's example is an image-to-CAD workflow: describe the object, model it, render the model, grade the rendering against the original image, fix the issues, repeat.

It is the only one of the four patterns with a feedback edge back to its own first step.

The evaluator half is a model grader — and it inherits the model grader's rule: ask it for strengths, weaknesses and reasoning, not a bare number. Feedback that says “6/10” gives the producer nothing to act on.

questions.q: Which workflow pattern has a feedback edge back to its own first step?
options: Parallelization
Chaining
Routing
Evaluator–optimizer
questions.explain: Rejection sends feedback back to the producer. The other three flow forwards only.

questions.q: What must the evaluator return for the loop to work?
options: A bare score, so acceptance is a simple threshold
Reasoning about strengths and weaknesses, not just a number — the producer needs something to act on
A rewritten version of the output
A confidence interval on its grade
questions.explain: It is a model grader, and the same rule applies: a bare number is uninformative and drifts to the middle.

reviewQuestions.q: In the image-to-CAD example, what is graded against what?
options: The CAD model against a specification document
A rendering of the model against the original image
The description against the image
The final model against a previous version
reviewQuestions.explain: Render, then compare the render to the original — a check in the same medium as the input.

knowledgePoints.name: The decision rule, and the four shapes
knowledgePoints.teach:
Given a scenario: if the steps are knowable in advance → design a workflow. If they are not, and the model must improvise across a flexible toolset → design an agent.

When the answer is workflow, pick by shape:

The scenario looks like…Pattern
independent evaluations to combine into one decisionParallelization
stages that build on each other; a prompt overloaded with rulesChaining
distinct categories, each needing different handlingRouting
quality that has to be iterated toward against criteriaEvaluator–optimizer

Two questions, in order. Which kind of thing, then which shape.

questions.q: What is the first question to ask of an orchestration scenario?
options: How many Claude calls will it need?
Are the steps knowable in advance?
Which model tier does it need?
Does it require tools?
questions.explain: Knowability first. Only once it is a workflow does the shape question apply.

questions.q: A scenario needs quality iterated toward against explicit criteria. Which pattern?
options: Parallelization
Chaining
Routing
Evaluator–optimizer
questions.explain: Criteria plus iteration until accepted is the evaluator–optimizer signature.

knowledgePoints.name: What you hand an agent
knowledgePoints.teach:
When the rule does land on agent, the design is not finished — it has just moved.

An agent is a goal plus a tool set. Claude figures out the combination of calls itself, including recognising when it needs more information from the user: asked to calculate a warranty expiry, it will ask for the purchase date rather than inventing one.

Design tools to be abstract and combinable, not hyper-specialised — the same principle, arrived at from the orchestration side.

Which closes the circle. The reason to prefer workflows is that agents have a lower success rate; the main lever you have on an agent's success rate is the quality and generality of its toolset.

questions.q: What do you actually hand an agent?
options: A sequence of steps and a tool set
A goal and a tool set
A goal and a maximum iteration count
A classified input and a specialised pipeline
questions.explain: Goal plus tools. If you could hand it steps, you would be building a workflow.

questions.q: An agent is asked to calculate a warranty expiry and lacks the purchase date. What is the expected behaviour?
options: It fails with an error
It asks the user for the purchase date
It assumes today's date
It calls every tool until one supplies a date
questions.explain: Recognising it needs more input is part of what an agent does — and a listed benefit of the approach.

reviewQuestions.q: A scenario describes triaging incoming documents into three types, each handled by a different specialised prompt. Which pattern?
options: Parallelization
Routing
Chaining
An agent
reviewQuestions.explain: Distinct categories, different handling, one branch each — routing.

reviewQuestions.q: A scenario says the system must handle requests the team cannot enumerate ahead of time, combining tools as needed. Workflow or agent?
options: Workflow — enumerate the common cases and default the rest
Agent — the steps are not knowable in advance
Workflow, using routing with an 'other' category
Either; the distinction is a matter of preference
reviewQuestions.explain: 'Cannot be enumerated ahead of time' is the rule's second branch, stated almost verbatim.
